summary: Markets are caught between relief and unease: a fragile pause in Middle East strikes is cooling oil prices even as a fresh wave of US tariffs and central banks moving in opposite directions reshape where money flows next.
causalChain: A pause in US-Iran strikes near the Strait of Hormuz knocked oil down over 7% and eased inflation fears, but that relief is colliding with new US tariffs hitting roughly 60 countries and central banks splitting paths (Japan and Europe leaning toward hikes, Australia leaning toward a cut, the US and Mexico holding steady), which is keeping currencies, bond yields, and crypto swinging as investors reprice where growth and rates head next.

drafts.text: Oil prices just fell more than 7% in a single day. Why? The US and Iran quietly stopped attacking each other for a second straight day, raising hope of a real ceasefire. Oil had jumped nearly 40% this month as fighting spread near the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, narrow sea lanes huge numbers of oil tankers must pass through. When those routes look dangerous, shipping oil gets riskier, so prices rise. Now that the shooting has paused, that fear is fading, and prices are dropping with it.

The US central bank meets this week to decide how expensive it is to borrow money across the economy. Most expect it to hold steady, the fifth meeting in a row with no change. But here is the twist: traders now think the next move could be to make borrowing MORE expensive, not less, since prices keep rising faster than the bank wants. That fear already shows in what the US government pays to borrow for 30 years, which has climbed to about 5.16%, a heavy bill taxpayers help cover for decades.

This past Friday the US added new import taxes of 10% to 12.5% on goods from 60 countries, basically every major trading partner it has. The stated reason is forced labor concerns, but the effect is the same as any tariff: foreign goods cost more to bring in, and firms often pass that cost to shoppers. Separately, Washington let its trade deal with Mexico and Canada start winding down after refusing to renew it, adding years of uncertainty for goods built with parts crossing those borders.

On Wednesday the US added a new 10 percent tax on many Mexican products entering the country. But goods covered by the North America trade deal, USMCA, skip that tax completely, and most of what Mexico ships to the US already qualifies. That is why, even as US and Mexican negotiators wrapped up three days of trade talks in Mexico City on Friday, the peso barely flinched. When almost all your exports are already covered by an existing deal, a tariff aimed at everyone else hits very little.

The Mexican peso closed the week near 17.48 to the US dollar, actually gaining a little, ranking among the five best performing major currencies that week. That is surprising, since the same days brought a new US tariff and tense trade talks over North America's trade deal, the kind of news that usually scares money out of a currency. Investors stayed put partly because Mexico's central bank pays a much higher interest rate than the US, and partly because the tariff hit less trade than feared.

Prices in Mexico rose 3.55 percent over the past year as of mid-June, the smallest increase since December 2020. That matters because Mexico's central bank had kept interest rates high specifically to fight fast-rising prices, and now that prices are cooling, the bank has stopped cutting and is holding steady at 6.50 percent instead of easing further. High rates make loans and credit cards pricier for regular people, so slower prices plus steady rates suggest the economy is settling down.

Japan's currency, the yen, has been sliding for months and just hit its weakest level in a broad measure against other currencies. Central bank officials are now talking about raising interest rates faster than expected, with a big decision meeting on July 31. Why does a weak yen matter? It makes things Japan buys from abroad, like oil, pricier, pushing up costs at home. Raising rates faster could make the yen stronger, but also make borrowing money costlier for Japanese businesses and shoppers.

South Korea's exports jumped about 60% in the first three weeks of July compared to last year, and Taiwan's export orders hit an all-time high too. The big reason: computer chips. Companies around the world are buying huge numbers of chips to build AI systems, and Korea and Taiwan make most of the world's advanced chips. This is a good sign these countries' factories are staying busy, and it hints that the AI spending boom by tech companies is still going strong, not slowing down.

Hong Kong's stock market, the Hang Seng index, dropped nearly 1% on Friday to end the week at about 24,963 points, dragged down by big Chinese tech companies like Alibaba and Tencent. Even so, the index is still up sharply over the past year and sits roughly in the middle of its 12-month trading range. The swings show investors are nervous about China's economy and trade tensions, even as money keeps flowing back into Hong Kong-listed stocks whenever confidence picks back up.

Europe's central bank left interest rates unchanged this week, holding its main rate at 2.25%. The backstory: after cutting rates for over a year, it reversed course in June and raised them for the first time since 2023. Why? Fighting flared up in the Middle East, oil prices jumped, and that pushed up what people pay for gas and everyday goods. Now the bank's chief hinted another hike could come in September, meaning loans and mortgages across Europe may stay expensive longer than hoped.

Germany's stock market jumped over 1 percent on Friday, and one company did most of the work: software giant SAP, up 10 percent after saying its cloud business is growing faster than expected. That single earnings report lifted the whole market even though oil just topped 100 dollars a barrel on Middle East tensions, and new US tariffs on European goods pushed borrowing costs to their highest in 15 years. One company's good news outweighed a country's bad news, at least for a day.

Britain's economy is quietly beating expectations: shoppers spent 1 percent more in June even though economists predicted a drop. Normally that means people expect the Bank of England to cut interest rates soon. Instead the opposite is happening: oil prices jumped on renewed Middle East fighting, stoking inflation fears, so investors now bet the Bank could raise rates twice by next March instead of cutting. That means pricier mortgages even as the economy looks strong.

Australia's central bank meets this Thursday, July 30, to decide on its main interest rate, which has sat at 4.35% since June. Many economists now expect a cut to 3.60%, ending a long stretch of high borrowing costs. Why: the pace of price increases across Australia has cooled sharply this year, so policymakers feel less need to keep loans expensive to slow the economy down. A cut would make home loans and business loans cheaper, and it usually gives a lift to stocks and house prices too.

Iron ore, the rock used to make steel, has been getting cheaper, recently trading around 99 dollars a ton. This matters because Australia's two biggest mining companies, BHP and Rio Tinto, earn much of their money digging up this rock and shipping it to China, the world's biggest steelmaker. China's steel mills are earning thinner profits as the country's construction industry, once the top buyer of steel, keeps shrinking. Even so, Rio Tinto just posted its highest iron ore sales in six years.

New Zealand's central bank raised its key interest rate this month for the first time since 2023, nudging it up a quarter point to 2.50%. It acted because rising gasoline and electricity costs have been pushing up everyday prices, and raising interest rates is the main tool central banks use to cool that down. Separately, the United States just added a new 12.5% tax on goods imported from New Zealand, tied to labor practice concerns, adding another headache for the country's exporters.

Bitcoin bounced back to about $65,300 on Monday, up 1.5%, after sinking to $64,000 on Friday. The move had little to do with crypto itself: the US said it would pause air strikes on Iran, easing war fears, so investors felt safer buying riskier assets again. Attention now turns to the Federal Reserve's meeting this week, deciding whether to raise interest rates. Higher rates make borrowed money pricier and tend to pull cash out of Bitcoin, so the decision could swing crypto sharply either way.

Funds that let ordinary investors buy Ethereum through a regular brokerage account took in about $337 million this month, ending an eight week stretch of investors pulling cash out. BlackRock's fund led the buying. This matters because these funds are mostly used by big institutional investors, and after two months of selling, a sudden return of buying suggests professional money managers think Ethereum's price, stuck near $1,850, may be close to a bottom.

The SEC, the top US securities regulator, plans to release three new rulebooks for crypto as soon as this month, covering how companies can sell crypto tokens, how brokers must safeguard customer coins, and how crypto trading platforms should operate. The goal is clear rules so crypto companies build in the US instead of overseas. Congress has its own crypto bill, but it likely will not get a vote before August, leaving the SEC's own rules to govern crypto for now.

Astronomers found a giant planet without ever seeing it, they smelled its air instead. Beta Pictoris, a star 63 light-years away, hides behind a dust cloud too thick to see through. Using the James Webb telescope, a UC San Diego team detected carbon monoxide, water, and methane, a planet's chemical fingerprint, confirming a hidden giant planet twice Jupiter's mass. 📄 Published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters · More: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/2041-8213/ae801b

Every koala alive today descends from survivors of a die-off that hit 100,000 years before humans reached Australia. Scientists at Sydney and Texas A&M measured how fast koala DNA mutates for the first time, then used that clock to rewind 457 genomes. Numbers crashed 100,000 years ago and bottomed out in an ice age, as a drying Australia split eastern and western koalas apart. 📄 Published in Molecular Biology and Evolution · More: https://academic.oup.com/mbe/article/43/6/msag108/8702405

Physicists built a machine with zero moving parts that steals energy from radio waves, mimicking what a spinning black hole is predicted to do with light. A CUNY team led by Andrea Alù built a ring of electronics that flicker in sequence, tricking incoming waves into acting like they hit an ultra-fast spinning object, then bouncing back out stronger, gaining real energy despite nothing physically spinning. 📄 Published in Nature · More: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10725-y

Oak trees keep pulling carbon dioxide from the air for months after they stop growing new wood. Columbia scientist Mukund Palat Rao tracked 137 oak forests using satellites, sensors, and tree rings back to 1950. Eastern oaks stop growing by July but keep photosynthesizing into October, and that after-growth absorption is 36 percent of their whole year's carbon uptake, a chunk climate models have been ignoring. 📄 Published in Science Advances · More: https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady7139
